Shai-Hulud payload files setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js written into node_modules AIInstallation High
Hunts the worm's install-stage artifacts: the two new files (setup.mjs dropper and Math_Symbol.js credential-stealer) being written inside a node_modules package directory. Every compromised package in the keyv family gained exactly these two filenames, making them a reliable on-disk indicator. Rationale: Uses the article's two exact dropped filenames (setup.mjs, Math_Symbol.js) constrained to node_modules; both are verbatim from the compromise and cross-confirmed as Shai-Hulud artifacts, giving an extremely low-FP on-disk indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package coincidentally naming a build helper setup.mjs inside its published tarball
  • Local developer git-cloning the compromised repo for analysis (files land on disk without npm install)
  • Backup/AV quarantine tooling re-writing the file path during scanning
  • Monorepo tooling copying package fixtures containing a same-named test file
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the containing package.json to get the package name and version and hash setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js; confirm the version matches a known-poisoned release. 2) Contain: quarantine the files, isolate the host, and delete the affected node_modules; block the package version in the internal registry/proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints and CI runners for the same two filenames, check whether Math_Symbol.js was executed (bun child process), and rotate every credential class the payload targets (npm, GitHub, AWS, Vault).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime fetched from oven-sh GitHub releases during npm install AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the worm's C2/staging step: setup.mjs silently downloading the Bun runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/ so it can execute the payload with a runtime other than the local Node. Flags outbound requests to that release path originating from a node/npm/bun process tree. Rationale: Uses the article's exact staging URL path (github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/) tied to a node/npm/bun parent process; a package install that pulls the Bun runtime mid-install is anomalous and specific to this worm. Datadog Sysmon netflow lacks URL paths so that field and Sigma are omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-detection/shai-hulud-worm/
ATT&CKT1105 T1620 T1102
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI job that legitimately installs Bun as a project runtime/tool
  • Corporate mirror or artifact proxy pre-caching Bun releases
  • Docker base-image builds that fetch Bun as a documented dependency
  • Engineer manually evaluating Bun on their workstation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun upgrade","install bun","setup-bun"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and whether the Bun fetch coincided with an npm install and a setup.mjs execution on the same host within seconds. 2) Contain: if correlated with setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js, isolate the host, terminate bun/node, and rotate exposed credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for bun.exe executing Math_Symbol.js and for outbound HTTP to a Vault endpoint (the payload's Vault token fallback), and review which package version triggered the download.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","bun.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession

| where Url has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\\bun(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*oven-sh/bun/releases/download*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.app Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Bun runtime executing Shai-Hulud Math_Symbol.js credential stealer AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access stage: the freshly downloaded Bun runtime executing Math_Symbol.js, the payload that harvests npm tokens from .npmrc, GitHub CLI tokens, AWS keys from ~/.aws/credentials, and the VAULT_TOKEN env var. Using Bun rather than the local Node is a defense-evasion tell, and the script name is verbatim from the campaign. Rationale: Combines the article's exact payload filename (Math_Symbol.js) with its exact evasion runtime (bun); Bun executing a package-dropped JS credential extractor is a near-zero-legitimate pattern and is the direct credential-access step described in the writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-detection/shai-hulud-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.005 T1528 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project genuinely running a script named Math_Symbol.js via Bun (extremely unlikely, but possible in a math/symbol-processing library)
  • Malware analyst detonating the payload with Bun in a lab
  • A red-team emulation of the Shai-Hulud chain during an authorized exercise
  • Security tooling replaying the sample for signature testing
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm bun.exe launched Math_Symbol.js and capture the parent chain (npm install -> node setup.mjs -> bun); collect the package name/version. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately and treat all locally reachable secrets as compromised — force-rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs/session/OIDC tokens, AWS access keys and session tokens, and the Vault token; revoke active sessions. 3) Hunt: check npm and GitHub audit logs for publishes or repo pushes made with the stolen tokens (worm self-propagation), review AWS CloudTrail for use of the leaked keys, and sweep other dev hosts/CI runners for the same bun+Math_Symbol.js execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Math_Symbol.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Math_Symbol.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

npm preinstall hook executing setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js (keyv/cacheable worm) AIInstallation High
Hunts the keyv/cacheable supply-chain worm's install-time execution: an npm/node/yarn/pnpm install lifecycle spawning the dropper setup.mjs or the second-stage Math_Symbol.js, or any process matching the published dropper hashes. This fires purely on `npm install` with no import, app-start, or user interaction. Rationale: Anchors on the two file names the worm injects into every poisoned package (setup.mjs dropper, Math_Symbol.js stage-2) chained to an npm/node/yarn/pnpm parent, plus the three published SHA256s — all extremely specific to this campaign; corroborated by Socket, Snyk and Upwind write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/inside-keyv-npm-compromise-preinstall-malware-trusted-provenance-ide-hooks/ • https://socket.dev/blog/popular-npm-packages-in-the-keyv-and-cacheable-namespaces-compromised-in-active-supply-chain • https://www.upwind.io/feed/keyv-supply-chain-compromise-an-npm-worm-that-takes-its-orders-from-an-ethereum-smart-contract
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate package with a benign postinstall/preinstall build script literally named setup.mjs
  • Internal monorepo tooling that runs a bundler stage called Math_Symbol.js (rare, effectively never)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
  • CI runner replaying a cached/pinned pre-compromise lockfile that still references a clean version
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("webpack","vite build","rollup") and SHA256 !in ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668","9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc","d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which npm package + version pulled the hook — inspect the process tree parent chain and the CWD/repo path; check package.json for a 'preinstall' pointing at setup.mjs. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner, revoke any npm, GitHub (gh), AWS, Vault and kube tokens reachable from that account, and quarantine keyv/cacheable/flat-cache/file-entry-cache from the internal registry. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the Bun download (UC2), credential-store reads (UC3) and planted .claude/.vscode hooks (UC4); enumerate all repos that installed the poisoned versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm","node","corepack.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js") and (ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" or ProcessCommandLine has "Math_Symbol.js"))
    or SHA256 in ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668","9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc","d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","corepack","yarn","pnpm") and (ActingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "Math_Symbol.js"))
    or SHA256 in ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668","9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc","d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

keyv worm loader pulling Bun 1.3.13 runtime from GitHub during install AICommand & Control High
Hunts the second stage of the keyv/cacheable worm where setup.mjs silently downloads a standalone Bun runtime (v1.3.13) from GitHub (github.com / objects.githubusercontent.com, oven-sh/bun release assets) to execute the Math_Symbol.js stealer. Pivots on a node/npm/bun process fetching a Bun release binary during an install. Rationale: The worm's dropper fetching a standalone Bun runtime from GitHub during npm install is the campaign's signature evasion (using an unexpected JS runtime to run the stealer); anchored on oven-sh/bun release-asset URLs and Bun v1.3.13 tied to a node/bun install-context process. Confirmed by Upwind and Socket analyses. Cross-checked against: • https://www.upwind.io/feed/keyv-supply-chain-compromise-an-npm-worm-that-takes-its-orders-from-an-ethereum-smart-contract • https://socket.dev/blog/popular-npm-packages-in-the-keyv-and-cacheable-namespaces-compromised-in-active-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately installing Bun via a project that vendors the runtime from GitHub release assets
  • node-based CI job downloading a GitHub-hosted binary as part of a normal build step
  • node fetching a package tarball hosted on github.com (common for git-dependencies)
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style tooling resolving a git+https dependency
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun upgrade","bun install") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "setup.mjs")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is an npm/node install lifecycle (not an interactive `bun upgrade`) and that the URL points at a Bun release asset; correlate with UC1 on the same host/timestamp. 2) Contain: block egress to the specific object URL, isolate the host, and treat any credentials on it as exposed. 3) Hunt: look for the downloaded bun binary on disk, subsequent Math_Symbol.js execution, credential-file reads (UC3), and outbound connections to Ethereum RPC / non-registry hosts the worm uses for C2.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","bun.exe","bun")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oven-sh/bun","bun-v1.3.13","githubusercontent.com") or RemoteUrl endswith "github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js","preinstall") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any ("oven-sh/bun","bun-v1.3.13","bun-linux","bun-darwin","bun-windows")
| where DstHostname has_any ("github.com","githubusercontent.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname, Url, DstHostname, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

| ContextImageFileName=/(node|bun|npm)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())

npm-install child process reading developer credential stores (keyv stealer) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Math_Symbol.js stealer harvesting credentials during install: a node/bun/npm process (spawned by an install lifecycle) touching .npmrc, ~/.aws/credentials, GitHub CLI hosts.yml, ~/.kube/config or ~/.vault-token. These files should never be accessed by a package install. Rationale: The stealer's documented targets (.npmrc, AWS creds, gh hosts.yml, kube config, Vault token) accessed by an install-spawned node/bun process is the campaign's credential-theft behaviour; the process-context constraint keeps it far tighter than a bare credential-file access rule. Confirmed by Upwind and cybersecuritynews reporting on the 728KB stealer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.upwind.io/feed/keyv-supply-chain-compromise-an-npm-worm-that-takes-its-orders-from-an-ethereum-smart-contract • https://cybersecuritynews.com/keyv-npm-package-compromised/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legit npm postinstall that writes an auth token to .npmrc for a private registry
  • AWS SDK-based node CLI tooling reading ~/.aws/credentials as designed
  • dev tooling that reads ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml to reuse a GitHub session
  • kubectl-wrapping node tool reading ~/.kube/config during a normal deploy
  • File-read telemetry gaps on Defender (reads not always logged) causing intermittent coverage
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login") and FolderPath has ".npmrc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the credential-file access with UC1/UC2 on the same host and within the install window; if the process chain is an npm/node install, treat as malicious. 2) Contain: immediately revoke and rotate every credential type touched (npm token, GitHub PAT/gh session, AWS keys, Vault token, kube credentials) and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/GitHub audit) for use of the exposed credentials from unusual IPs, and enumerate other developer/CI hosts that installed the poisoned packages.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","npm.exe","npm")
| where FolderPath has_any (".npmrc","\\.aws\\","/.aws/","hosts.yml","\\.kube\\","/.kube/",".vault-token")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js","preinstall") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (".npmrc","/.aws/","\\.aws\\","hosts.yml","/.kube/","\\.kube\\",".vault-token")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

keyv worm planting .claude / .vscode auto-run hooks in project (agentic dev target) AIInstallation High
Hunts the worm's second execution path: setup.mjs writes .claude (Claude Code) and .vscode config files (settings/tasks/mcp/hooks) into the project so code runs the moment a developer or coding agent opens it — no npm install required. Pivots on a node/bun/npm process creating those config files. Rationale: This is the article's 'thesis' behaviour — the worm plants .claude/.vscode auto-run config to detonate on IDE/agent open — and is highly specific: an npm-install-spawned node/bun process writing agent/editor config is not normal package behaviour. Confirmed by The Hacker News and Snyk's keyv deep-dive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/keyv-linked-npm-worm-poisons-hundreds.html • https://snyk.io/blog/inside-keyv-npm-compromise-preinstall-malware-trusted-provenance-ide-hooks/
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legit scaffolding tool (create-*, generators) writing .vscode/settings.json or tasks.json into a new project
  • An IDE extension installer that legitimately provisions .vscode config via a node helper
  • A team's project template that ships .claude/settings.json checked in and rewritten on install
  • Prettier/ESLint config-sync tooling touching .vscode recommendations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("create-","yo ","degit","scaffold") and FolderPath has "\\.vscode\\" and FolderPath !has "\\.claude\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written .claude/.vscode file and inspect for hook/task commands that spawn shells, download, or run node/bun; check whether the writing process chains back to an npm install (UC1). 2) Contain: quarantine the repo, remove the malicious config, isolate the host, and warn any developer/agent not to open the project until cleaned. 3) Hunt: sweep all repos on the host and shared storage for identical .claude/.vscode hook content, and check whether a coding agent already executed it (subsequent node/bun/shell children of the IDE).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\.claude\\","/.claude/","\\.vscode\\","/.vscode/")
| where FileName in~ ("settings.json","settings.local.json","tasks.json","mcp.json","hooks.json")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","npm.exe","npm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.claude\\","/.claude/","\\.vscode\\","/.vscode/")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("settings.json","settings.local.json","tasks.json","mcp.json","hooks.json")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate

keyv/cacheable npm compromise: node executing preinstall setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js dropper AIInstallation High
Hunts the Mini Shai-Hulud preinstall dropper shipped in the compromised keyv, cacheable, flat-cache, file-entry-cache and ecto npm releases (Aug 4 2026). Fires when node runs the malicious lifecycle script setup.mjs under an npm/pnpm/yarn install, or when any process references the unique second-stage filenames Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact lifecycle-hook string ('preinstall':'node setup.mjs') plus the byte-identical second-stage filenames Math_Symbol.js and math_init.js, which are unique to this campaign and not benign npm artifacts. Cross-checked Aikido, Wiz and Snyk advisory SNYK-JS-KEYV-18515941. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/large-scale-npm-pypi-supply-chain-campaign-suspected-across-multiple-popular-packages
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate unrelated package that genuinely ships a benign setup.mjs preinstall script (rare, but exists) run under npm
  • Internal monorepo tooling that names a build script setup.mjs and invokes it via node during install
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
  • A developer manually running 'node setup.mjs' for a non-malicious project of their own
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" and not (FolderPath has "node_modules") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the hitting host, pull the full node process tree and confirm the working directory is inside node_modules for keyv/cacheable/flat-cache/file-entry-cache/ecto; hash the on-disk setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js and compare to the campaign SHA256s. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/CI runner from network, kill the node and any bun child process, and treat all developer/CI-scoped tokens as exposed — DO NOT revoke GitHub tokens yet if gh-token-monitor is present. 3) HUNT: Search the org's lockfiles and private mirrors for the affected versions, look for bun download from GitHub, .claude/.vscode hook files, and gh-token-monitor persistence before rotating credentials from a clean system.

keyv npm compromise: malicious payload file drop by SHA256 (setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js) AIDelivery Medium
Highest-fidelity detection for the keyv/cacheable compromise: matches the two byte-identical payload files by their published SHA256 across every affected release, or the unique second-stage filenames written into node_modules. Snyk confirmed all nine retrievable tarballs carried the identical 29,918-byte setup.mjs and 727,680-byte Math_Symbol.js. Rationale: Uses the article's exact published SHA256 values for the 29,918-byte setup.mjs and 727,680-byte Math_Symbol.js — Snyk verified these are identical across all affected releases, so a hash match is a confirmed compromise regardless of which package name delivered it. Corroborated by Aikido and Wiz. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel or EDR feed writing the sample to disk during automated IOC ingestion
  • A malware analyst intentionally staging the file in a lab
  • A backup/restore job re-materializing a quarantined copy of the payload
  • An unrelated legitimate file coincidentally named math_init.js under node_modules (mitigated by requiring the hash for the strongest signal)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the SHA256 match is a true hit (hash match = confirmed campaign payload); identify which package/version under node_modules delivered it and whether this is a dev workstation or CI runner. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, quarantine the file, and inventory which credentials that identity could reach (GitHub/npm tokens, cloud creds, kubeconfig, Vault). Disable gh-token-monitor persistence BEFORE revoking any GitHub token. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the delivering package name across all repos/lockfiles/mirrors, pin to last-known-good (e.g. flat-cache 6.1.23, cacheable-request 13.0.19, cache-manager 7.2.9), and rotate all exposed secrets from a clean host.

keyv npm compromise: IDE-hook persistence files planted in .claude / .vscode AIInstallation High
Detects the second execution path from GitHub commit d8c850c7 — malicious setup.mjs / math_init.js written into a repo's .claude or .vscode directory so a Claude SessionStart command or a VS Code folderOpen task auto-runs the payload when a developer or coding agent opens the checkout. A .mjs/init script inside these config dirs is abnormal. Rationale: Anchors on the exact artifact set from GitHub commit d8c850c7 (.claude/setup.mjs, .claude/math_init.js, .vscode/setup.mjs) — an executable .mjs/init script inside IDE/agent config directories is not a normal project layout and represents the workspace-trust execution path the article highlights. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately stores a helper setup.mjs inside .vscode for local task automation (uncommon but possible)
  • A developer copying a template repo that includes .vscode task scripts
  • IDE extension scaffolding that writes .mjs helpers into .vscode
  • Git clone/checkout materializing these files from a trusted internal repo (verify provenance before dismissing)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the flagged .claude/.vscode file and check for obfuscated loader content or references to Math_Symbol.js/math_init.js/Bun; identify the repo and whether it was opened in an IDE or coding agent (VS Code folderOpen / Claude SessionStart). 2) CONTAIN: Remove the hook files, revoke workspace trust for the repo, and isolate the host if the task/SessionStart already fired (correlate with node/bun process events). 3) HUNT: Grep all internal repos for .claude/.vscode setup.mjs, review recent commits by the compromised maintainer identity, and check for gh-token-monitor persistence and Bun downloads on the same host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.mjs","math_init.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

keyv npm compromise: Bun runtime executing second-stage math_init.js / Math_Symbol.js AICommand & Control High
Detects the loader's second execution stage — when Bun is absent the loader fetches Bun 1.3.13 from GitHub and uses it to run the 727,680-byte second stage (Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js). A bun process executing these filenames, especially spawned by a node setup.mjs parent, is high-signal for this campaign. Rationale: Uses the article's specifics: the loader fetches Bun 1.3.13 and runs the second stage named math_init.js / Math_Symbol.js. Bun executing those exact filenames, or Bun spawned by a setup.mjs parent, is not a normal developer pattern. Corroborated by Upwind's execution-flow write-up ('bun run index.js' second stage). Cross-checked against: • https://www.upwind.io/feed/large-scale-npm-pypi-supply-chain-campaign-suspected-across-multiple-popular-packages • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1587.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Bun-native project that legitimately has a source file named math_init.js (mitigated by requiring the setup.mjs parent or exact campaign filenames)
  • A developer who genuinely uses Bun and just installed it from GitHub
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample
  • CI pipeline that legitimately runs bun against a project script (verify parent is not setup.mjs)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the bun parent chain traces to node setup.mjs / an npm install of an affected package; check for a freshly downloaded bun binary in temp and outbound connections to github.com for the Bun 1.3.13 release. 2) CONTAIN: Kill the bun process, isolate the host, and treat GitHub/npm tokens, cloud creds, private keys, DB strings, Vault and Kubernetes SA tokens as harvested — disable gh-token-monitor before revoking GitHub tokens. 3) HUNT: Look across the fleet for bun-spawned-by-setup.mjs, the campaign payload hashes, and IDE-hook files; rotate all reachable secrets from a clean system.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")

keyv npm compromise: gh-token-monitor credential-persistence artifacts (macOS/Linux) AIInstallation High
Detects the gh-token-monitor persistence dropped by the Mini Shai-Hulud second stage — a monitor that watches a stolen GitHub token and runs a supplied handler when the token stops working. Fires on creation of gh-token-monitor.sh, the ~/.config/gh-token-monitor directory, or a process referencing gh-token-monitor. CRITICAL: this persistence must be disabled before any GitHub token revocation. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named persistence mechanism (gh-token-monitor) and the artifact names corroborated by Wiz/Upwind (~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh, ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/). The name is unique to this malware family and carries the critical operational caveat to disable it before token revocation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.upwind.io/feed/large-scale-npm-pypi-supply-chain-campaign-suspected-across-multiple-popular-packages • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1546.004 T1543 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A homegrown ops script legitimately named gh-token-monitor (extremely unlikely given the exact name)
  • A researcher recreating the persistence artifact in a lab
  • A backup restoring a previously infected home directory
  • Endpoint IOC-sweep tooling writing the filename into a report path under a scan directory
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Locate gh-token-monitor.sh and ~/.config/gh-token-monitor plus any LaunchAgent/systemd unit referencing it; confirm which GitHub token it is watching. 2) CONTAIN: Disable and remove the monitor and its LaunchAgent/systemd service FIRST, then isolate the host — revoking the GitHub token before disabling the monitor can trigger the malware's handler. 3) HUNT: After the monitor is neutralized, rotate the exposed GitHub/npm tokens, cloud creds, private keys and Vault/K8s tokens from a clean system, and sweep the fleet for the payload hashes, bun second-stage execution, and IDE-hook files.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "gh-token-monitor.sh"
   or FolderPath has "gh-token-monitor"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "gh-token-monitor.sh" or TargetFilePath has "gh-token-monitor"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Sequelize Oracle SQLi: TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP quote-bypass payload in HTTP request AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP query strings / bodies carrying the CVE-2026-69240 payload shape — a parameter value beginning with TO_DATE( or TO_TIMESTAMP( followed by a quote break-out (||'', OR 1=1, --, UNION). This is the delivery vector that reaches Sequelize's vulnerable escape() path in the Oracle dialect. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC signature from the GHSA (`TO_DATE('0','Y')||'' OR 1=1--`): a param value opening with TO_DATE(/TO_TIMESTAMP( plus a break-out token. Legitimate query params never combine an Oracle date-cast function with `||''`/`OR 1=1`/`--`, making this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/sequelize/CVE-2026-69240/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-SEQUELIZE-2959225 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-69240
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DAST/pentest tooling (sqlmap, Burp Scanner, Acunetix) firing SQLi payloads during authorized testing
  • An internal application that legitimately accepts Oracle TO_DATE(...) expressions as a search parameter (rare)
  • Security awareness / red-team exercises replaying known CVE payloads
  • WAF that decodes and logs the raw attack even though it blocked the request (still a true attempt, triage as such)
  • Copy/paste of Oracle SQL snippets into a free-text search field by a developer
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("<known-scanner-ip-placeholder>") // replace/remove if no sanctioned scanners; prefer excluding by scanner UserAgent when available
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (SrcIP, UriPath, Query) and confirm the target app uses Sequelize with dialect=oracle and version < 6.37.4; check the HTTP status/response size to judge whether injection succeeded. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, add a virtual-patch rule dropping TO_DATE(/TO_TIMESTAMP( in user input, and prioritise upgrading Sequelize to >= 6.37.4. 3) Hunt: pivot on SrcIP for other endpoints/params hit, and cross-check the Oracle audit UC (below) for the same window to confirm the payload actually executed at the DB.
union
 (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=cIP, Host=Computer, Method=csMethod, UriPath=csUriStem, Query=csUriQuery, Status=tostring(scStatus)),
 (AppServiceHTTPLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=CIp, Host=CsHost, Method=CsMethod, UriPath=CsUriStem, Query=CsUriQuery, Status=tostring(ScStatus)),
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=SourceIP, Host=DestinationHostName, Method=RequestMethod, UriPath=RequestURL, Query=RequestURL, Status=tostring(EventOutcome))
| where Query has_any ("TO_DATE","TO_TIMESTAMP","to_date","to_timestamp")
| where Query matches regex @"(?i)(TO_DATE|TO_TIMESTAMP)\s*[\(%]"
| where Query has "||" or Query contains "%7C%7C" or Query matches regex @"(?i)\bor\b\s+1\s*=\s*1" or Query has "UNION" or Query contains "--"
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-69240")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-69240")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AnyDesk silent/unattended install used for DragonForce access · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

RDP re-enable + EDR/Defender disable batch script (LockBit intrusion) AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-access batch script observed in the leaked-LockBit-builder case that enabled RDP by setting fDenyTSConnections to 0 and disabled endpoint defenses before ransomware deployment. Anchors on the exact registry value/data pair the article's script wrote. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim registry write from the article's disable-defenses batch script (HKLM\...\Control\Terminal Server \ fDenyTSConnections = 0) which turns RDP on; pairs it with reg.exe execution to keep fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-builder-leaked-online-by-angry-developer/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately enabling RDP on a new server build via a provisioning script
  • GPO/DSC/Intune configuration baseline that manages fDenyTSConnections
  • MSP onboarding automation that turns on RDP for remote management
  • Server 2016 role-setup wizards that toggle Remote Desktop
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","omadmclient.exe","gpscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating account and parent process of the reg.exe/registry write; confirm whether the same host also saw EDR/Defender service stops in the surrounding minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the account used to write the value, and re-set fDenyTSConnections to 1 if the change was unauthorized. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account across DeviceLogonEvents for RDP (LogonType 10) and search for PsExecSvc.exe/named ransomware payloads (1.exe, LBB.exe) and Defender-tamper events fleet-wide.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Terminal Server"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "fDenyTSConnections"
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SystemSettings.exe","ServerManager.exe","mmc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"
| where CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections" and CommandLine has_any ("/d 0","/d 0x0")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LockBit payload execution via PsExec service (PsExecSvc.exe → 1.exe/LBB.exe) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the manual lateral deployment of the custom LockBit build from the leaked builder: the sample was configured without psexec_netspread, so operators used PsExec (PsExecSvc.exe) to remotely launch ransomware binaries named 1.EXE and LBB.exe. Targets the impact/deployment step, not generic PsExec admin use. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim payload names (1.EXE, LBB.exe) and the PsExecSvc.exe service the operators relied on for manual spread after building a variant without psexec_netspread; combining parent + payload names keeps the otherwise-generic 1.exe fidelity acceptable. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/lockbit-3-0-based-custom-targeted-ransomware/112375/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1486 T1569.002 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin using Sysinternals PsExec for remote software rollout (PsExecSvc.exe as parent)
  • Automation/RMM that names a tool 1.exe in a temp build path
  • Software packaging test binaries transiently named 1.exe
  • Remote patch scripts pushed via PsExec across a fleet
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\SCCM\\","\\ccmcache\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 and full path of the spawned binary and the source host driving PsExecSvc.exe; check for mass DeviceFileEvents FileRenamed/FileModified bursts on the same device. 2) Contain: network-isolate affected hosts, block the payload hash, and disable the deploying account. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host where PsExecSvc.exe appeared (USN Journal .KEY artifacts corroborate historic spread), look for kill_defender/Defender-uninstall events and wallpaper/registry changes indicative of LockBit encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "PsExecSvc.exe"
    or FileName in~ ("1.exe","LBB.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\PsExecSvc.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\1.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\LBB.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Potato privilege-escalation tooling (GodPotato / SweetPotato / BadPotato) AIExploitation High
Hunts the SeImpersonate token-abuse tools the article attributes to the observed privilege-escalation activity in these intrusions. Anchors on the exact tool family names used to move from a service/valid account to SYSTEM. Rationale: Anchors on the three Potato variant names the article explicitly attributes to privilege escalation (GodPotato, SweetPotato, BadPotato); these are offensive-only tool names, so name/cmdline matches are high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/
ATT&CKT1134.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / pentest engagement running Potato tools with authorization
  • Security researcher detonating the tools in a sandbox VM
  • A file legitimately containing the substring 'potato' in an unrelated business name (rare, mitigated by path/cmdline context)
  • Malware-analysis training lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Tools\RedTeam\", @"\PurpleTeam\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating (pre-escalation) account and whether the resulting process/child ran at SYSTEM integrity; review parent process (often a service or web-app pool identity). 2) Contain: isolate the host and reset credentials for the abused service/valid account. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for follow-on SYSTEM-level actions — Defender-disable batch scripts, RDP enablement (fDenyTSConnections=0), PsExec spread, and ransomware payload drops.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
    or CommandLine has_any ("GodPotato","SweetPotato","BadPotato")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk silent/unattended install used for DragonForce access AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the attacker-driven AnyDesk deployment the article ties to DragonForce (Case 02): AnyDesk installed and configured for unattended access to give operators remote control before ransomware. Anchors on the unattended-install command-line flags rather than mere presence of AnyDesk. Rationale: Anchors on AnyDesk (named in Case 02 as the DragonForce remote-access vector) combined with unattended-install flags that legitimate interactive users rarely pass, corroborated by DragonForce write-ups documenting silent AnyDesk installs for persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/dragonforce-ransomware-attack/ • https://www.intel471.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware
ATT&CKT1219 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk legitimately deploying AnyDesk unattended via GPO/RMM
  • MSP standardizing on AnyDesk for remote support with --start-with-win
  • User self-installing AnyDesk from a legit MSI that passes --silent
  • Vendor support session where AnyDesk is provisioned with a set password
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the installing account and parent process (deployment tool vs. email client vs. script) and whether AnyDesk is a sanctioned tool for this host/OU. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill AnyDesk, and rotate credentials; capture the AnyDesk ID/anydesk.trace for the incoming operator IP. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents for AnyDesk relay traffic (boot.net.anydesk.com / *.relay), then look for DragonForce indicators — PsExec spread, mass encryption, ransom notes — across hosts that ran AnyDesk in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "AnyDesk.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install","--silent","--start-with-win","--set-password","--get-id")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\AnyDesk.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--install","--silent","--start-with-win","--set-password")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-03 10 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Explore how passkey implementation gaps undermine security when relying parties fail to validate the User Verified flag, reducing MFA to a single factor. The post Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication appeared first on Unit 42 .
